title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 12)
summary: NH continues his reading of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations, covering why insults from unskilled people only hurt if you let them, detachment from one's name and fame, virtue over bodily pleasure, the external origin of evil, and consistency of values regardless of circumstances. He ties these to lifting: excuses to skip training reveal the commitment was never real.
claims: Insults usually come from people below you who want to drag you down; ignoring them saves your energy and may push them to improve
Paying attention to insults, even silently, gives the insulter power over you
NH doesn't feel attached to his name; it is just a code, and attachment to name is attachment to fame
Be wary of religions that promise a better afterlife, because it can stop people improving themselves on earth
People with virtues should express and exemplify them despite the modern shaming of morals
Once you have a life goal, direct every action, thought and word toward it
Bodily pleasure is immediate while the soul's reward is delayed, so pursuing pleasure traps you and prevents elevation
Most evil comes from environment and upbringing, not birth, and can only affect you if you invite it in
People who skip training the moment an obstacle appears (car breaks, so no gym) were looking for an excuse; bike or run there instead
Giving up a principle when it becomes inconvenient means it was never yours; consistency is what makes others follow your example
Develop a self before over-socializing; people socialized too early feel alone among many friends
Stay curious; cynicism comes from no longer seeing the sparkle in life
